farraa:14-14.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱلْقَنَاطِيرِ ٱلْمُقَنْطَرَةِ﴾: the singular of القناطير is قِنطار. It is said that it is the fill of an ox-hide of gold or silver. (القناطيرُ) [in the nominative] is permissible in ordinary speech. القناطير are three, and المقنطرة are nine. That is what I heard, and it means the multiplied.

farraa:15-15.t:
His saying: ﴿قُلْ أَؤُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِخَيْرٍ مِّن ذٰلِكُمْ﴾, then He said ﴿لِلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَوْا عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ جَنَّاتٌ﴾: He put الجنات in the nominative (rafʿ) by the lām. It was not permissible to refer it back to the beginning of the speech [i.e. to make it genitive after بخير], because you have placed the lām between the two, and a genitive-governing particle cannot be implied when the lām stands between them. It is, however, permissible to interpose the lām and its like between the governor of the nominative and what it puts in the nominative, and between the governor of the accusative and what it puts in the accusative.
So you say: رأيت لأخيك مالا، ولأبيك إبلا ("I saw wealth belonging to your brother, and camels belonging to your father"). And you put [the noun] in the nominative by the lām when you do not make the verb govern; and in the nominative: قد كان لأخيك مال ولأبيك إبل. But it is not permissible to say in the genitive: قد أمرتُ لك بألف بألف ولأخيك ألفين while you mean (بألفين), because implying the genitive-governing particle is not permissible. Do you not see that you say: مَنْ ضربتَ؟ ("Whom did you strike?") and he says: زيدا; and مَن أتاك؟ ("Who came to you?") and he says: زيدٌ? Thus the governor of the nominative and of the accusative is implied. But if he said: بمن مررت؟ ("By whom did you pass?"), you would not say: زيدٍ, because the genitive-governing particle together with what it governs is like a single word. If you put before [the lām] what you had placed after the lām, the genitive becomes permissible in it, because it is like something coordinated (mansūq) onto what precedes it when you have not placed anything between them. So if الجنّات were put before the lām, and it were said: (بخَيْرٍ مِنْ ذَلِكُمْ جناتٍ للذين اتقوا), the genitive would be permissible, and the accusative too, in the sense of repeating the verb with the bāʾ dropped; as the poet said:
أتيتَ بعبدالله فى القِدّ مُوثَقا * فهلا سعِيدا ذا الخيانةِ والغدرِ
(You brought ʿAbd Allāh bound in a rawhide thong — why not Saʿīd, the man of treachery and betrayal?)
That is what you do with a verb that takes the bāʾ: when both are implied together, [the noun] is put in the accusative, as when you say: أخاك ("your brother!") meaning امْرُرْ بأخيك ("pass by your brother"). And the poet said, [in] permitting the coordination when you put it first and place nothing between them:
ألا يا لقومٍ كُلُّ ما حُمَّ واقع * ولِلطيرِ مَجْرىً والجُنُوبِ مَصَارع
(O people! All that is decreed comes to pass; the birds have their course, and the flanks [of the slain] have their places of falling.)
He meant: وللجنوبِ مصارع; he allowed himself to drop the lām, and by it مصارع is in the nominative, since he did not place anything between them. Had you said: (ومصارعُ الجنوبِ) intending to imply the lām, it would not be permissible.
And another said:
أوعدنى بالسجن والأداهِم * رِجلِى ورِجلى شَثْنَة المناسِمِ
(He threatened me with prison and with fetters — my foot; and my foot is rough-soled.)
He meant: أوعد رجلى بالأداهم ("he threatened my foot with fetters").
And His saying: ﴿فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ وَمِنْ وَرَاء إسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ﴾: the best way is the nominative for يعقوب.
Whoever reads it in the accusative intends the accusative by it; the genitive is not permissible except by repeating the bāʾ: ومن وراء إسحاق بيعقوب.
And any two things that come together, [one of them] having come before the genitive noun in which you consider the implication [of the particle] permissible, follow this pattern. And do not mind whether you separate the two by an agent, a direct object or an adjective. Among examples of that is that you say: مررت بزيد وبعمرو ومحمد [or] وعمرو ومحمد. But it is not permissible to say مررت بزيد وعمرو وفى الدار محمدٍ until you say: بمحمد. Likewise: أمرت لأخيك بالعبيد ولأبيك بالوِرِق ("I ordered slaves for your brother and silver coin for your father"); and it is not permissible to say: لأبيك الوِرِق. Likewise: مُرَّ بعبدالله موثَقا ومطلقا زيدٍ ("Pass by ʿAbd Allāh bound, and by Zayd free") while you mean: ومطلقا بزيد. But if you say: وزيدٍ مطلقا, that is permissible, on the analogy of coordination (nasaq), since you have not placed anything between the two.
And His saying: ﴿قُلْ أَفَأُنَبِّئُكُمْ بِشَرّ مِن ذَلِكُمُ النارُ وَعَدها الله الَّذِينَ كَفَروا﴾: there are three ways in it. The best of them is the nominative; and the accusative from two directions: from وعدها, since النار would then not be a mubtadaʾ (subject); and the other accusative by making the "informing" fall on it through the dropping of the genitive particle. That is permissible because you have not placed any barrier between them. And the nominative is as a mubtadaʾ.
If you ask: then what do you say about the poet's words:
آلآن بعد لجاجتى تَلْحَوْننِى * هلا التقدّمُ والقلوبُ صِحاحُ
(Now, after my persistence, you blame me? Why not [your] going ahead while hearts were sound?)
— by what is التقدّم in the nominative? I say: by the sense of the wāw in his saying (والقلوبُ صحاح), as if he said: العِظَة والقلوب فارغة ("admonition, while hearts are empty"), والرُطَبُ والحرّ شديد ("fresh dates, while the heat is intense"); then you bring هلاّ in upon it while it remains as you put it in the nominative. And you could put التقدّم in the accusative by intending a verb, as you say: أتيتنا بأحاديث لا نعرفها فهلا أحاديثَ معروفة ("You brought us stories we do not know; why not well-known stories?").
And if you made the lām in His saying ﴿لِلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَوْا عِندَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ part of the ṣila (complement) of the "informing", the genitive of الجنات, الأزواج and الرضوان would be permissible.

farraa:16-16.t: His saying: ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ﴾: if you wish, you make it genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of للذين اتقوا; and if you wish, you begin it afresh and put it in the nominative, since it is a verse, and what it qualifies is in a verse before it. Similar to it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿إنّ اللهََ اشْتَرَى مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنينَ أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ﴾; when the verse ended He said ﴿التّائِبُونَ الْعَابِدُونَ﴾, and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd] it is "التائِبين العابدين".

farraa:17-17.t: Likewise ﴿ٱلصَّابِرِينَ وَٱلصَّادِقِينَ﴾: their position is genitive, and had they been nominative it would have been correct. And His saying ﴿وَٱلْمُسْتَغْفِرِينَ بِٱلأَسْحَارِ﴾: those who pray in the hours before dawn; and he says: prayer before dawn is the best of the times of prayer. Muḥammad ibn al-Jahm informed us: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us: Sharīk narrated to me from al-Suddī concerning His saying ﴿سَوْفَ أَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ رَبِّى﴾: he said: he deferred them until the time before dawn.

farraa:18-19.t:
His saying: ﴿شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لاَ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ﴾: the readers have read the alif of (أنه) with fatḥa, and also in His saying "أنّ الدِّينَ عِنْدَ اللّهِ الإِسْلاَمُ".
If you wish, you take (أنه) as a condition, and make the witnessing fall on His saying ﴿إِنَّ الدِّينَ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلإِسْلاَمُ﴾; the first (أنّ) then admits the genitive, as when you say: شهد الله بتوحيده أن الدين عنده الإسلام ("Allah bore witness, by His oneness, that the religion with Him is Islam"). «[Translator's note: the source has كقلوك, evidently a misprint for كقولك "as when you say".]»
If you wish, you begin (إِن الدين) afresh with kasra and make the witnessing fall on ﴿أَنَّهُ لاَ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ﴾. That is how Ḥamza read it, and it is the more preferable of the two ways to me. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "إن الدين عند الله الإسلام". Al-Kisāʾī used to read both with fatḥa.
Ibn ʿAbbās read the first with kasra and with fatḥa "أن الدين عند الله الإسلام", and that is a good way: he made ﴿أَنَّهُ لاَ إِلَـٰهَ إِلاَّ هُوَ﴾ resumptive and parenthetical — as if a fāʾ were intended in it — and made the witnessing fall on "أن الدين عند الله". Similar to it in ordinary speech is your saying to a man: أشهد - إنى أعلم الناس بهذا - أنّك عالم ("I bear witness — I am the most knowing of people about this — that you are learned"), as if you said: أشهد - إنى أعلم بهذا من غيرى - أنك عالم. And when you bring two أنّ clauses on which knowledge, witnessing, supposing or the like has fallen, you put kasra on one of them and fatḥa on the one on which the supposing or knowing or the like falls. You say to a man: لا تحسبن أنك عاقل؛ إنك جاهل ("Do not suppose that you are intelligent; you are ignorant"), because you mean فإنك جاهل. And if the fāʾ is suitable in the preceding إن, you put kasra on it and fatḥa on the second. What comes [of this kind] is to be measured by this.
And His saying ﴿وَأُوْلُواْ ٱلْعِلْمِ قَآئِمَاً بِٱلْقِسْطِ﴾: it is accusative on qaṭʿ (detachment), because it is an indefinite qualifying a definite. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "القائِمُ بالقسط", nominative, because it is a definite qualifying a definite.

farraa:20-20.t:
His saying: ﴿فَإنْ حَآجُّوكَ فَقُلْ أَسْلَمْتُ وَجْهِيَ للَّهِ وَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَنِ﴾ — ﴿وَمَنِ ٱتَّبَعَنِ﴾: the Arabs, concerning the yāʾs that come at the ends of words — such as اتبعن، أكرمن، أهانن, and like His saying "دَعْوَةَ الدّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ - وَقَدْ هَدَانِ" — sometimes drop the yāʾ and sometimes keep it. Whoever drops it is content with the kasra before it as an indication of it. That is because it is like an extension (ṣila): since it is quiescent at the end of the word and was felt heavy, it was dropped. Whoever pronounces it in full, that is the [original] structure and the base form. They also do that with the yāʾ even when no nūn precedes it; they say هذا غلامى قد جاء and غلامِ قد جاء ("this is my servant; he has come"). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿فَبَشِّرْ عِبادِ الَّذِينَ﴾, outside the vocative, with the yāʾ dropped. Most often it is dropped with the possessive in the vocative; because the vocative is much used in speech, it was [also] dropped outside the vocative. Ibrāhīm said ﴿رَبَّنَا وتَقَبَّل دُعَاءِ﴾ without yāʾ, and He said in Sūrat al-Mulk ﴿كَيْفَ كَانَ نَكِير﴾ and "نذِير"; that is because they are verse-endings, and the verses before them had no second yāʾ, so they were made to follow what precedes them, since that is part of the speech of the Arabs.
They also do that with a radical yāʾ; they say هذا قاض ورام وداع ("this is a judge, an archer, a caller") without yāʾ; they do not keep the yāʾ in any [indefinite] form of the pattern fāʿil. When they add the alif and lām to it, they say it both ways: they keep the yāʾ and they drop it. Allah said ﴿من يهدِ الله فهو المهتدِ﴾, throughout the Qur'an without yāʾ.
But He said in al-Aʿrāf "فهو المهتدى". Likewise He said ﴿يَوْمَ يُنَادِى المُنَادِ﴾ and ﴿أُجيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدّاعِ﴾. The preferable thing to me is to keep the yāʾ with the alif and lām, because its dropping in قاض and مفترٍ and the like is due to its meeting the nūn of declension (tanwīn), which is quiescent while the yāʾ is quiescent; joining two quiescents was not acceptable, so the yāʾ was dropped because of its quiescence. When you add the alif and lām, adding the nūn is not permissible, and that is why I prefer keeping the yāʾ. Whoever drops it considers this reason: he says, "I found the word without yāʾ before the alif and lām were in it, so when they entered I disliked adding to it what had not been there." And all of it is correct.
And His saying ﴿وَقُلْ لِّلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلْكِتَابَ وَٱلأُمِّيِّينَ أَأَسْلَمْتُمْ﴾: it is a question, and its meaning is a command. Similar to it is the saying of Allah ﴿فهل أَنْتُم مُنتهون﴾, a question whose interpretation is: "Desist!" Likewise His saying ﴿هل يَسْتَطِيع ربُّك﴾ and هل تستطيع رَبَّك is only a request. Do you not see that you say to a man: هل أنت كافّ عنا؟ ("Will you leave us alone?"), meaning: "Leave us alone!"; and you say to a man: أين أين؟ ("Where? Where?"), [meaning]: "Stay and do not leave!" For that reason the question was given a conditional answer (jawāb) just as the command is given one. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَى تِجَارَةٍ تُنْجِيكُم مِنْ عَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ. آمِنوا", so he explained (هل أدلكم) with the command.
In our reading it is in the form of a statement. So the conditional answer in our reading is on His saying (هل أدلكم), and the conditional answer in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh is on the command, because that is the explanation.

farraa:21-21.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَكْفُرُونَ بِآيَاتِ ٱللَّهِ وَيَقْتُلُونَ ٱلنَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ وَيَقْتُلُونَ﴾: it is read ويقتلون, and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "وقاتلوا"; that is why those who read it read (يقاتلون). Al-Kisāʾī read it for a long time as (يقاتلون), then went back on it; I reckon he saw it in some of the copies of ʿAbd Allāh as ﴿وقَتَلوا﴾ without the alif, so he abandoned it and returned to the reading of the general body [of readers], since the written text agreed with the meaning of the reading of the general body.

farraa:25-25.t:
His saying: ﴿فَكَيْفَ إِذَا جَمَعْنَاهُمْ لِيَوْمٍ لاَّ رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾: it was said with the lām, and (فى) may also be suitable in its place. You say in ordinary speech: جُمِعوا لِيوم الخميس ("they were gathered for Thursday"). It is as if the lām belongs to an implied verb on Thursday; as if they were gathered for what will happen on Thursday.
When you say: جمعوا فى يوم الخميس ("they were gathered on Thursday"), you do not imply a verb. And in His saying ﴿جَمَعْنَاهُمْ لِيَوْمٍ لاَّ رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ [the meaning] is: for the reckoning and the recompense.

farraa:26-26.t:
His saying: ﴿قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ مَالِكَ ٱلْمُلْكِ﴾ — ﴿اللهم﴾ is a word the Arabs pronounce with fatḥa. Some grammarians have said: it was given fatḥa only because the two mīms were added to it, since it is not called with يا as you say يا زيد and يا عبدالله; so the mīm in it was made a substitute for يا. Yet someone recited to me:
وما عليكِ أن تقولى كُلَّما * صلَّيتِ أو سبَّحتِ يا اللهمَّ ما * اُردُدْ علينا شيخنا مسلما *
(What harm is there for you to say, whenever you pray or glorify: "O Allāhumma, return our old man to us safe and sound"?)
And we have not found the Arabs adding such a mīm to defective nouns except unstressed (single), as in الفم, ابنم and هم. We consider that it was a word to which أُمّ was joined: you mean يا ألله اُمّنا بخير ("O Allah, aim us toward good"); it became frequent in speech and the two were blended. So the ḍamma that is on the hāʾ comes from the hamza of أُمّ: when [the hamza] was dropped, [its vowel] moved to what precedes it. And we consider that the Arabs' saying (هَلُمَّ إلينا) ("come to us") is like it: it was only (هل), and أُمّ was joined to it, and it was left with its fatḥa. Some of the Arabs, when they drop the mīm, say: يا ألله اغفر لى and يا الله اغفر لى ("O Allah, forgive me"); they pronounce its alif with hamza and they also drop it. Whoever drops it follows the regular course, because it is an alif and lām like [the article in] الحارث among names. Whoever pronounces it with hamza imagines that it is part of the word, since it does not fall away from it. Someone recited to me:
مباركٌ هُوّ ومَن سمَّاه * على اسمك اللهمَّ يا ألله
(Blessed is he, and whoever named him, in Your name, Allāhumma, O Allah.)
(اللهم) has become so frequent in speech that its mīm has been lightened in some dialects; someone recited to me:
كَحَلْفَةٍ من أبى رياح * يسمعها اللهمَ الكُبار
(Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ, which Allāhumma, the Great, hears.)
The common recitation is: لاهه الكبار. And al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
* يسمعها الله والله كبار *
(Allah hears it, and Allah is great.)
And His saying, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿تُؤْتِى المُلْكَ مَنْ تَشَاءُ﴾. (When you see مَن تشاء together with "whom You will": "from whom You will to take it away"). «[Translator's note: this parenthetical sentence is garbled in the source; it appears to explain the parallel phrase وتنزع الملك ممن تشاء as "from whom You will to take it away from him".]» The Arabs are content with what appeared at the beginning of the speech, of what ought to appear after شئت. They say: خذ ما شئت ("take what you wish"), and كن فيما شئت ("be in whatever you wish"), meaning: in whatever you wish to be in. So the verb after it is dropped. The Exalted said: "اعملوا ما شِئتم", and the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿فى أىّ صورةٍ مّا شاء ركّبك﴾, the meaning being — and Allah knows best —: in whatever form He willed to compose you, He composed you. And from it is His saying, Exalted: ﴿وَلَوْلاَ إذْ دَخَلْتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلْتَ ما شَاءَ الله﴾. Likewise all of the conditional: إن شئت فقم، وإن شئت فلا تقم; the meaning is: if you wish to stand, stand; and if you wish not to stand, do not stand. Allah said ﴿فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِنْ ومَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾; this makes clear that the willing falls on belief and disbelief, and both are left unexpressed. For that reason the Arabs said: (أَيُّها شئت فلك) ("whichever of them you wish is yours"), putting أيّ in the nominative, because they meant: whichever of them you wish to be yours is yours. And they said (بِأيِّهم شئت فمرّ) ("pass by whichever of them you wish"), meaning: by whichever of them you wish to pass, pass.

farraa:27-27.t:
His saying: ﴿تُولِجُ ٱللَّيْلَ فِي ٱلْنَّهَارِ وَتُولِجُ ٱلنَّهَارَ فِي ٱلْلَّيْلِ﴾: the exegesis came that it is the shortening of the night being made to enter the day, and likewise the day is made to enter the night, until the length of the one and the shortness of the other reach their limit.
And His saying ﴿وَتُخْرِجُ ٱلْحَيَّ مِنَ ٱلْمَيِّتِ﴾: it is mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās that it is the egg: it is dead, and the chick comes out of it alive; and the sperm-drop: it is dead, and the child comes out of it.

farraa:28-28.t:
His saying: ﴿لاَّ يَتَّخِذِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ is a prohibition, and it is put in the jussive (majzūm) in that case. And [it would be permissible] if it were put in the nominative as a statement, as some read: ﴿لاَ تُضَارُّ وَالِدَةٌ بِوَلَدِها﴾. «[Translator's note: the source sentence breaks off without its main clause; "it would be permissible" is implied.]»
And His saying ﴿إِلاَّ أَن تَتَّقُواْ مِنْهُمْ تُقَاةً﴾: this is the most common usage of the Arabs, and the readers have read it so. It is mentioned of al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid that they read "تَقِيَّة". And all is correct.

farraa:29-29.t: His saying: ﴿يَعْلَمْهُ ٱللَّهُ﴾ is jussive as the conditional answer (jazāʾ). ﴿وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي ٱلأَرْضِ﴾ is nominative as a fresh beginning (istiʾnāf); as Allah said in Sūrat Barāʾa ﴿قاتِلوهم يعذِّبْهم الله﴾, putting the verbs in the jussive, then said ﴿ويتوبُ الله على من يشاء﴾, nominative as a fresh beginning. Likewise His saying ﴿فإن يشأ الله يختِمْ على قلبِك﴾, then He said ﴿ويمح الله الباطِل﴾: ويَمْحُ is intended as a nominative fresh beginning, even though it has no wāw [at the end]; the wāw was dropped from it just as it was dropped in His saying ﴿سندعُ الزّبانية﴾. When you coordinate onto the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), the nominative, the accusative and the jussive are all permissible. As for His saying ﴿وإن تبدوا ما فِى أنفسِكم أو تخفوه يحاسِبْكم بِهِ الله فيغفِرُ﴾, it is read jussive by coordination, and also with a sukūn resembling the jussive while it is intended as nominative: the rāʾ of يغفر is assimilated into the lām, and the bāʾ of يعذب into the mīm; just as it is said ﴿أرَأَيْتَ الذِى يُكذِّب بِالدّين﴾, and as al-Ḥasan read ﴿شهر رمضان﴾ [with assimilation].

farraa:30-30.t:
His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَجِدُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ مَّا عَمِلَتْ مِنْ خَيْرٍ مُّحْضَراً﴾: ما is in the sense of الذى (the relative "that which"). It cannot be conditional, because (تجد) has fallen on ما [as its object].
And His saying ﴿وَمَا عَمِلَتْ مِن سُوۤءٍ﴾: you also refer it back to (ما), making (عملت) its ṣila (relative clause), in the sense of the nominative, because of His saying ﴿تَوَدُّ لَوْ أَنَّ بَيْنَهَا﴾. Were you to begin it afresh and not make (تجد) fall on it, the conditional would be permissible; you would make (عملت) jussive [in position]. And one says for تودّ: تودَّ with fatḥa, and تودِّ [with kasra]. Were the doubling overt, تَوْدَدْ would be permissible. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "وما عملت من سوء ودَّت", and this is evidence for the jussive [conditional]; but I have not heard any of the readers read it in the jussive.

farraa:33-33.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱصْطَفَىٰ آدَمَ وَنُوحاً وَآلَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَآلَ عِمْرَانَ عَلَى ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾: it is said [that it means] He chose their religion above all religions, because they were Muslims. Similar to it, among cases where something is implied and then dropped, is His saying ﴿واسألِ القرية التِى كنا فيها﴾.
Then He said ﴿ذرية بعضها مِن بعضٍ﴾, putting الذرّية in the accusative in two ways. One of them is that you make الذرّية a qaṭʿ (detachment) from the nouns before it, because they are definite. And if you wish, you put it in the accusative by repetition [of the verb]: اصطفى ذرّية بعضها من بعض ("He chose offspring, one from another"). Had you begun it afresh and put it in the nominative, it would have been correct.

farraa:35-35.t: His saying: ﴿إِنِّي نَذَرْتُ لَكَ مَا فِي بَطْنِي مُحَرَّراً﴾: for the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis): I will not occupy him with anything else.

farraa:36-36.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ﴾: it may be part of Maryam's statement, so that it is "والله أعلم بِما وضعْتُ" with the ʿayn made quiescent, and some of the readers read it so; and it may be from the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in which case you make the tāʾ quiescent (jazm), because it is a statement about an absent female.

farraa:37-37.t: His saying: ﴿وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا﴾: whoever reads it with shadda puts زكريا in the position of the accusative, as when you say: ضمَّنها زكريا ("he made Zakariyyā responsible for her"); and whoever reads the fāʾ without shadda puts زكرياء in the position of the nominative. There are three dialectal forms of زكريا: shortening its alif, so that neither nominative nor accusative nor genitive appears in it; lengthening its alif, so that it takes the accusative and the nominative without nūn, because it is not declined fully (a diptote); and much of the speech of the Arabs drops the lengthening and the quiescent yāʾ, so that it is said: هذا زكرىّ قد جاء ("this is Zakariyy; he has come"), and it is declined fully, because it resembles the relative adjectives (nisba) among Arab names. «[Translator's note: the source has حاء, a misprint for جاء "has come".]»

farraa:38-38.t:
His saying: ﴿هَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنْكَ ذُرِّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً﴾: الذرّية is a plural, and it may have a singular meaning. This is one such case, because he said: ﴿فهب لِى مِن لدنك ولِيا﴾ and did not say أولياء. It was said "طيبة" and not طيبا only because الطيبة was made to follow the form of the word الذرّية, so it was made feminine for its being feminine. Had it been said ذرّية طيبا, it would have been correct.
Similar to it in the speech of the Arabs is the poet's saying:
أبوك خليفةٌ وَلَدتْه أخرى * وأنت خليفة ذاك الكمال
(Your father is a caliph whom another [caliph, fem.] begot, and you are a caliph — that is perfection.)
He said (أخرى) because the noun الخليفة is feminine [in form], and the proper way would be to say: وَلَدَه آخر. And another said:
فما تزْدَرِى من حَيَّة جَبَليّةٍ * سُكَاتٍ إذا ماعَضّ ليس بأدْرَدَا
(What do you despise in a mountain snake, silent, which when it bites is not toothless?)
He said جَبَليّة, making it feminine for the femininity of the noun الحيّة, then he made it masculine when he said إذا ما عضَّ and did not say عضّت; he went by the masculine sense. And another said:
تَجوبُ بنا الفلاةَ إِلى سعِيدٍ * إذا ما الشّاةُ فى الأَرطَاة قالا
(She crosses the desert with us toward Saʿīd, when the wild ox takes its midday rest in the arṭā-bush.)
This kind is permissible only with a noun to which "so-and-so" (فلان) does not apply, such as الدابّة, الذرّية and الخليفة. If you name a man with any of these, so that it has the sense of فلان, it is not permissible to make its verb or its adjective feminine. So you say in that case: حدّثنا المغيرة الضّبىّ ("al-Mughīra al-Ḍabbī narrated to us"), and الضّبيّة is not permissible; nor is it permissible to say حدّثَتْنا, because it is in the sense of فلان and not of فلانة. As for his saying:
وعنترةُ الفلحاء جاء مُلأَّماً * كأنَّهُ فِنْدٌ من عَمَاية أَسود
(And ʿAntara of the split lip came fully armoured, as if he were a black crag of [Mount] ʿAmāya.)
he said الفلحاء, qualifying him by his lip. He said: I heard Abū Tharwān say of a man of Ḍabba who had large eyes: هذا عينان قد جاء ("here comes 'two eyes'"), making it like an adjective for him. And one of the Bedouins said of a man with a broken front tooth: قد جاءتكم القَصْماء ("the broken-toothed one [fem.] has come to you"), going by his tooth.

farraa:39-39.t:
His saying: ﴿فَنَادَتْهُ الْمَلَئِكَةُ﴾ is read with the masculine and with the feminine. Likewise the verb of الملائكة and similar plurals is made feminine and masculine. The readers read "يعرج الملائكة" and "تعرج", and "تتوفاهم" and "يتوفاهم الملائكة", and all is correct. Whoever uses the masculine goes by the masculine sense; whoever uses the feminine does so for the femininity of the noun, and because the feminine applies to a group of men, women and others. The angels in this place are Jibrīl, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, alone. That is permissible in Arabic: to speak of a single one in the manner of the plural; as you say in ordinary speech: خرج فلان فى السُفُن ("so-and-so went out in the ships") when he went out in only one ship, and خرج على البغال ("he went out on the mules") when he rode only one mule. And you say: مِمَّن سمعت هذا الخبر؟ ("From whom did you hear this news?") and he says: من الناس ("from people"), when he heard it from only one man. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has said: ﴿وإذا مَسَّ النّاسَ ضُرّ﴾ and ﴿وإذا مسَّ الإنسان ضر﴾, and their meaning — and Allah knows best — is one. That is permissible where one particular individual is not intended.
And His saying ﴿وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي فِي ٱلْمِحْرَابِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ is read with kasra, but the fatḥa in it is better in Arabic. Whoever gives (أنّ) fatḥa makes the calling fall on it, as if he said: they called him with this: that Allah gives you good tidings. Whoever gives it kasra says: calling is of the nature of saying, and saying is reported speech (ḥikāya), so put kasra on إنّ in the sense of reported speech. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "فناداه الملائكة وهو قائم يصلِّى فى المحراب يا زكريا إن الله يبشرك". When the calling falls on an overt addressee, like (يا زكريا) and its like, you put kasra on (إن), because the reported speech becomes pure when what contains (يا) is addressed with it; neither nominative nor accusative reaches it. Do you not see that you say: يا زيد إنك قائم ("O Zayd, you are standing"), and يا زيد أنك قائم is not permissible? But when you say ناديت زيدا أنه قائم ("I called out to Zayd that he is standing"), putting (زيدا) in the accusative by the calling, it is permissible to make the calling fall on (أنّ) as you made it fall on زيد. It is not permissible to give إنّ fatḥa when you say يا زيد, because no known accusative [governor] has fallen on زيد. And He said in Ṭā Hā: ﴿فلّما أتاها نودِى يا موسى إِنى أنا ربك﴾, so (إِنى) was given kasra. Had it been given fatḥa, it would have been correct in two ways. One of them is that you make the calling fall on (أنّ) alone, with nothing implied in it, so (أنّ) is in the position of the nominative [as deputy agent]. And if you wish, you make the name of Mūsā implied in (نودى), and (أنّ) is in the position of the accusative, meaning: بأنى أنا ربك ("with: I am your Lord"); when you remove the bāʾ, you put it in the accusative. And if it were said in ordinary speech: نودى أنْ يا زيد ("it was called out: O Zayd"), making (أن يا زيد) [what is in the nominative by the calling], it would be correct, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿وناديناه أن يا إبراهيم. قد صدّقت الرؤيا﴾.
This is what applies to the calling when you make (إن) fall [after] يا زيد is said; it is as if you said: he was called with this call. When you make it fall on a noun by the verb, you give أن fatḥa and you give it kasra. And when you add to the calling, which the verb has reached, an addressed noun, you may introduce (أن) with it and say ناديت أن يا زيد; and you may remove it from (يا زيد) and place it in the verb after it, and then put it in the accusative [i.e. give it fatḥa]. And kasra is permissible as reported speech. Among what strengthens the view of those who allowed "إن الله يبشرك" with kasra as reported speech is His saying: ﴿ونادَوا يا مالك ليقض علينا ربك﴾, and He did not say: أن ليقض علينا ربك; this is the way of reported speech. And He said in another place ﴿ونادى أصحابُ النار أصحابَ الجنة أن أفيضوا﴾, and did not say: أفيضوا; this is a command and that is a command; so that you may know that both ways are correct. And "يبشرك" was read [without shadda] by the companions of ʿAbd Allāh in five places of the Qur'an: two words in Āl ʿImrān, and in Banī Isrāʾīl, in al-Kahf and in Maryam. Both the light and the doubled forms are correct. It is as if the doubled form refers to the good tidings of the bearers of good tidings, and the light form comes from the sense of gladdening and delighting. This is something the elder masters used to say. One of the Arabs recited to me:
بَشَرتُ عِيالى إذْ رأيت صحيفةً * أتتك من الحَجَّاج يُتْلى كتابُها
(I gladdened my household when I saw a document that came to you from al-Ḥajjāj, its writing being read out.)
Some of them said: أبشرت; perhaps it is a Ḥijāzī dialect. I heard Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna mention it as يُبْشِر. بشرت is a dialect form I heard from ʿUkl, and al-Kisāʾī related it from others. Abū Tharwān said: بَشرَنى بوجه حسن ("he gladdened me with a pleasant face"). And al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
وإذا رأيت الباهشين إلى العلى * غُبْرا أكفُّهم بِقاع ممحِل
فأَعِنْهُمُ وابْشَرْ بما بَشِرُوا به * وإذا همُ نزلوا بضَنْك فانزِل
(When you see those who reach eagerly for high things, their hands dusty in a barren plain, help them, and rejoice in what they rejoice in; and when they halt in hardship, halt with them.)
And the rest of the Qur'an is read with shadda according to the companions of ʿAbd Allāh and others.
And His saying: ﴿يُبَشِّرُكَ بِيَحْيَـىٰ مُصَدِّقاً﴾: (مصدّقا) is accusative because it is indefinite and يحيى is definite.
And His saying: ﴿بكلمة﴾ means: confirming ʿĪsā.
And His saying: ﴿وَسَيِّداً وَحَصُوراً وَنَبِيّاً﴾ are referred back to His saying: مصدّقا. It is said that الحَصُور is the one who does not approach women.

farraa:41-41.t: His saying: ﴿أَلاَّ تُكَلِّمَ ٱلنَّاسَ﴾: if you intend the pure future, you put (تكلِّم) in the accusative and take (لا) not in the sense of ليس. If you mean: your sign is that you will be in this state for three days, you put it in the nominative and say: أن لا تكلِّمُ الناس; do you not see that it is good to say: آيتك أنك لا تكلم الناس ثلاثة أيام إلا رمزا ("your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days except by gesture")? Gesture (الرمز) is with the lips, the eyebrows and the eyes, and mostly with the lips; all of that is رَمْز.

farraa:45-45.t:
His saying: ﴿إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱلْمَلاۤئِكَةُ يٰمَرْيَمُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكِ بِكَلِمَةٍ مِّنْهُ ٱسْمُهُ﴾: it belongs to what I mentioned to you about His saying ﴿ذُرّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً﴾: (اسمه) was said in the masculine according to the meaning; had it been made feminine, as He said ﴿ذُرّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً﴾, it would have been correct.
And His saying (وَجِيهاً) is a qaṭʿ (detachment) from عيسى; had you put it in the genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of الكلمة, since it is ʿĪsā, it would have been correct.

farraa:46-46.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِي ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلاً﴾: الكهل is referred back to الوجيه. ﴿وَيُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ﴾: had there been in place of (ويكلّم) the word ومكلما, it would have been accusative. The Arabs put يفعل and فاعِل together when they occur in coordinated phrases in speech. The poet said:
بِتّ أعَشِّيها بغَضْبٍ باتِرِ * يقصِد فى أَسْوُقِها وجائِر
(I spent the night feeding them [the camels] at night with a cutting sword, striking straight at their shanks and going astray.)
And another said:
من الذَّرِيحيَّات جَعْدا آرِكا * يقصُر يمشى ويطول باركا
(Of the Dharīḥī camels, curly-haired, grazing on arāk; he is short when walking and tall when kneeling.)
As if he said: short when walking, tall when kneeling. So likewise (فَعَلَ), when it is in the position of a ṣila [qualifying clause] for an indefinite, has (فاعِل) made to follow it, and is made to follow (فاعِل). You say in ordinary speech: مررت بفتىً ابنِ عشرين أو قد قارب ذلك ("I passed by a youth twenty years old, or who has nearly reached that"), and مررت بغلام قد احتلم أو محتلمٍ ("I passed by a boy who has reached puberty, or pubescent"). The poet said:
يا ليتنى عَلِقْتُ غير خارج * قبل الصباح ذاتَ خَلْقٍ بارِج * أُمّ الصبىّ قد حبا أو دارج *
(Would that I had attached myself, not going out before morning, to a woman of fine form, mother of a child that has crawled or is toddling.)

farraa:49-49.t:
His saying: ﴿كَهَيْئَةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ﴾: it refers to the clay. In al-Māʾida ﴿فتنفخ فيها﴾ it refers to the form (الهيئة), so it is feminine for its femininity. In one of the two readings it is (فأنفخها), and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh (فأنفخها) without فى. That is like what the Arabs say: ربّ ليلة قد بِتّ فيها وبِتُّها ("many a night have I spent in it, and spent it").
It is also said with the verb:
* ولقد أَبيت على الطَوَى وأظلهُّ *
(I spend the night in hunger, and spend the day in it.)
Prepositions are dropped, even though they differ with nouns and verbs. «[Translator's note: الصفات here is al-Farrāʾ's Kufan term for prepositions.]» The poet said:
إذا قالت حذامِ فأنصِتوها * فإن القول ما قالت حذام
(When Ḥadhāmi speaks, listen to her, for the true word is what Ḥadhāmi says.)
And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, who is most truthful in speech, said: ﴿وإِذا كَالُوهُمْ أَو وَزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرون﴾, meaning: كالوا لهم ("they measured for them"). And the poet said:
ما شُقّ جَيْب ولا قامتك نائحة * ولا بكتك جِياد عند أسلابِ
(No collar was rent, nor did a mourning woman stand [in lament] for you, nor did fine steeds weep for you beside the spoils.)
And His saying (وما تدَّخِرون) is تفتعلون from ذخرت ("I stored"). It is also read (وما تدْخَرون), light, on the pattern تَفْعَلون. Some of the Arabs say تدَّخِرون [sic], making the dāl and the dhāl alternate in تفتعلون from ذخرت; and with ظلمت one says مظّلِم and مطَّلِم, and مُذَّكِر and مدَّكِر. I heard some of Banū Asad say: قد اتَّغر ("he has lost his milk teeth"), and this dialect form is common among them in particular; others say: قد اثَّغر. «[Translator's note: the second تدَّخِرون is presumably meant as تذَّخِرون with dhāl; the source prints it with dāl.]»
As for those who say يدّخر, يدّكِر and مدّكِر: they found that when the tāʾ is quiescent and is met by a dhāl, the tāʾ enters into the dhāl and becomes a dhāl. They disliked that the tāʾ should become a dhāl so that the iftiʿāl form could not be recognised in it, so they looked for a letter that would be a middle point between the two in nearness, and put it in place of the tāʾ and in place of the dhāl.
As for those who made the dhāl prevail, they carried the analogy through and paid no attention to its being a single letter; so they assimilated the tāʾ of iftiʿāl to the dhāl, the tāʾ and the ṭāʾ.
And do not deny their choosing a letter between two letters, for they said ازدجر, whose [underlying] meaning is ازتجر; they made the dāl a middle point between the tāʾ and the zāy. Some of them have said مُزجَّر, making the zāy prevail just as [others] made the tāʾ prevail. I heard one of Banū ʿUqayl say: عليك بأبوال الظِباء فاصَّعِطْها فإنها شِفاء للطَحَل ("Take gazelles' urine and snuff it, for it is a cure for spleen disease"); he made the ṣād prevail over the tāʾ. The tāʾ of iftiʿāl becomes ṭāʾ with ṣād and ḍād; that is the eloquent usage, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿فَمَن اضْطُرّ فى مَخْمَصَةٍ﴾, whose meaning is iftaʿala from الضرر (harm). And Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said ﴿وأْمُرْ أهْْلَكَ بالصَّلاَةِ واصْطَبِرْ عَلَيْها﴾; so they made the tāʾ a ṭāʾ in iftiʿāl.

farraa:50-50.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمُصَدِّقاً﴾: (مصدّقا) is accusative by the verb (جئت), as if He said: وجِئتكم مصدّقا لِما بين يدىّ من التوراة ("and I have come to you confirming what was before me of the Torah"). Its accusative does not follow His saying (وَجِيهاً), because if it were so it would have been (ومصدّقا لما بين يديه).
And His saying: ﴿وَلأُحِلَّ لَكُم﴾: the wāw in it is like His saying ﴿وكذَلِكَ نُرِى إِبرَاهِيمَ مَلَكُوتَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ وَلِيَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُوقِنِين﴾.

farraa:52-52.t:
His saying: ﴿فَلَمَّآ أَحَسَّ عِيسَىٰ مِنْهُمُ ٱلْكُفْرَ﴾: He is saying: ʿĪsā found. الإحساس is finding [i.e. perceiving]; you say in ordinary speech: هل أحسست أحدا ("Did you perceive anyone?").
Likewise His saying ﴿هل تُحِسُّ مِنْهُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ﴾.
When you say حَسَسْت, without alif, it has the sense of annihilating and killing. Of that is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإذْنِهِ﴾. And الحَسّ is also tenderness and compassion, as in the saying of al-Kumayt:
هل مَنْ بكى الدار راجٍ أن تحِسّ له * أو يُبْكِىَ الدارَ ماءُ العَبْرةِ الخَضِل
(Does one who weeps over the abode hope that it will feel tenderness for him, or that the wet water of tears will make the abode weep?)
I heard one of the Arabs say: ما رأيت عُقَيليّا إلا حَسَست له ("I never saw a man of ʿUqayl without feeling tenderness for him"); and حسِست is a dialect form.
The Arabs say: من أين حَسَيت هذا الخبر؟ meaning: "Where did you learn this news?" [And sometimes they say حسِيت بالخبر and أحسيت به, replacing the sīn with yāʾ], as in the saying of Abū Zubayd:
* حسِينَ بِه فَهُنّ إليه شُوس *
(They sensed him, and so they look at him askance.)
The Arabs may also say: ما أحَستْ بهم أحدا, dropping the first sīn; and likewise in وددت, مسِست and هَمَمْت. He said: someone recited to me:
هل ينفَعَنْك اليوم إِن هَمْت بِهَمّْ * كثرةُ ما تأتى وتَعْقاد الرَتَمْ
(Will it benefit you today, if you are set on a purpose, how much you come and go and the tying of the ratam-threads?)
And His saying: ﴿مَنْ أَنصَارِيۤ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ﴾: the exegetes say: "who are my helpers with Allah?", and that is a good interpretation. It is only permissible to put (إلى) in the place of (مع) when you join one thing to another that was not with it, as the Arabs say: إن الذود إلى الذود إبل ("a small herd added to a small herd makes camels"), i.e. when you join a small herd to a small herd it becomes a [large] herd of camels. But when one thing is already with another, إلى is not suitable in the place of مع. Do you not see that you say: قدم فلان ومعه مال كثير ("so-and-so arrived with much wealth"), and you do not say in this case: قدِم فلان وإليه مال كثير? Likewise you say: قدم فلان إلى أهله ("so-and-so came to his family"), and you do not say: مع أهله. From it is His saying: ﴿وَلا تَأْكُلُوا أمْوالَهُمْ إِلَى أَمْوالِكُمْ﴾, meaning: do not add their wealth to your wealth.
The disciples (الحواريُّون) were ʿĪsā's close companions. Likewise the term الحواريّون applies to the close companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Al-Zubayr was called the ḥawārī of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and in the ḥadīth the term ḥawārī sometimes occurs for Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and their like. It came in the exegesis that they were called ḥawāriyyūn for the whiteness of their garments.

farraa:54-54.t:
The meaning of His saying: ﴿وَمَكَرُواْ وَمَكَرَ ٱللَّهُ﴾: this was revealed concerning ʿĪsā, when they wanted to kill him. He entered a house in which there was a skylight, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, had supported him with Jibrīl ﷺ, who raised him to heaven through the skylight. A man from among them entered upon him to kill him, and Allah cast the likeness of ʿĪsā son of Maryam upon that man. When he entered the house and did not find ʿĪsā in it, he went out to them saying: "There is no one in the house," and they killed him, thinking that he was ʿĪsā.
That is His saying ﴿وَمَكَرُواْ وَمَكَرَ ٱللَّهُ﴾. Plotting (المكر) from Allah is leading on step by step (istidrāj), not like the plotting of created beings.

farraa:55-55.t:
His saying: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يٰعِيسَىٰ إِنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ﴾: it is said that this involves something put first and something put later. Its meaning is: I am raising you to Myself, purifying you from those who disbelieve, and taking you in death after I send you down into the world. That is one interpretation.
The speech may also be without anything put first or later, in which case the meaning of متوفّيك is: taking you; as you say: توفيت مالى من فلان ("I received my money in full from so-and-so"), i.e. I took it from him. So التوفّى would be his being taken and raised to Him without death.

farraa:59-59.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ﴾: this was in response to the Christians' saying that he is His son, since he had no father. So Allah — Blessed and Exalted be He, greatly exalted — revealed ﴿إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ﴾, who had neither father nor mother, so he is a more wondrous case than ʿĪsā. Then He said: ﴿خَلَقَهُ﴾ — not that His saying "خلقه" is a ṣila (qualifying clause) for آدم; ṣilas belong only to indefinites, as when you say: رجل خلقه من تراب ("a man whom He created from dust"). Rather, He explained the matter of Ādam when He struck him as a likeness, and said "خلقه" as a detached explanatory clause. Similar to it is His saying ﴿مَثَلُ الذين حُمِّلوا التّوْرَاة ثم لم يَحْمِلُوهَا كَمَثَل الْحِمَارِ﴾, then He said ﴿يَحْملُ أَسْفَاراً﴾; الأسفار are books of knowledge which it carries without knowing what is in them. And if you wish you make "يحمل" a ṣila for الحمار, as if you said: كمثل حمار يحمل أسفارا ("like a donkey carrying books"), because what has the alif and lām may be qualified by a clause, so it is said: لا أمرَّ إلا بالرجل يقول ذلك ("I pass only by the man who says that"), like your saying بالذى يقول ذلك. But it is not permissible with زيد or عمرو to be qualified by a clause in the way a word with the alif and lām is.

farraa:60-60.t: His saying: ﴿ٱلْحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّكَ﴾: you put it in the nominative by implying (هو). Similar to it in al-Baqara: ﴿الْحَقُّ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾, i.e. it is the truth, or that is the truth, so do not doubt.

farraa:64-64.t:
His saying: ﴿تَعَالَوْاْ إِلَىٰ كَلِمَةٍ سَوَآءٍ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكُمْ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "إلى كلمة عدل بيننا وبينكم" ("to a just word between us and you"). In the sense of عدل (just, equitable) one also says سِوىً and سُوىً. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said in Sūrat Ṭā Hā ﴿فاجْعَلْ بَيْنَنَا وبَيْنَكَ مَوْعِداً لا نُخْلِفُهُ نَحْنُ وَلاَ أَنْتَ مَكَاناً سِوىً﴾ and سُوىً; by it is meant a just and fair [place] between us and you.
Then He said ﴿أَلاَّ نَعْبُدَ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهَ﴾: أن is in the position of the genitive in the sense: "come to [this]: that we worship none but Allah". And [it would be permissible] if you put (ما نعبد) in the nominative together with what is coordinated with it, with the intention: "come, let us make a pact: we do not worship any but Allah", because the meaning of الكلمة is a saying; it is as if you reported: "come, let us say: we worship none but Allah". «[Translator's note: the conditional sentence lacks its main clause in the source; "it would be permissible" is implied.]» And if you put the coordinated items in the jussive, that would be acceptable by tawahhum (assumed construction), because the speech would be jussive if أن were not in it, as you say: تعالوا لا نقل إلا خيرا ("come, let us say nothing but good").
Similar to it, among what follows the interpretation [rather than the form], is ﴿قُلْ إِنِّى أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ أَوَّلَ مَنْ أَسْلَمَ ولا تَكُونَنّ﴾: He made (ولا تكونن) a prohibition in the position of the jussive, while the first is accusative. Similar is ﴿وَأُمِرْنَا لِنُسْلِمَ لِرَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ. وَأَنْ أَقِيمُوا الصَّلاَةَ﴾: He referred أن back to the lām of purpose (lām kay), because (أن) is suitable in the place of the lām. So He referred أن back to [the lām], since [a word like] أن is suitable in the place of the lām. Do you not see that He said in one place ﴿يُرِيدُونَ لِيُطْفِئُوا﴾ and in another place ﴿يُرِيدُونَ أَنْ يُطْفِئُوا﴾?

farraa:65-65.t: His saying: ﴿لِمَ تُحَآجُّونَ فِيۤ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾: the people of Najrān said: "Ibrāhīm was a Christian, following our religion," and the Jews said: "He was a Jew, following our religion." So Allah gave them the lie and said ﴿وَمَآ أُنزِلَتِ ٱلتَّورَاةُ وَٱلإنْجِيلُ إِلاَّ مِن بَعْدِهِ﴾, i.e. after Ibrāhīm by a long age; then He rebuked them further.

farraa:66-67.t:
He said: ﴿هٰأَنْتُمْ هَؤُلاۤءِ حَاجَجْتُمْ﴾ to the end of the verse. Then He made that clear.
He said: ﴿مَا كَانَ إِبْرَاهِيمُ يَهُودِيّاً وَلاَ نَصْرَانِيّاً وَلَكِن كَانَ حَنِيفاً مُّسْلِماً﴾ to the end of the verse.

farraa:70-70.t: His saying: ﴿لِمَ تَكْفُرُونَ بِآيَاتِ ٱللَّهِ وَأَنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾: He is saying: you bear witness that Muḥammad ﷺ is [described] with his attributes in your Book. That is His saying: (تشهدون).

farraa:71-71.t: His saying: ﴿لِمَ تَلْبِسُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ بِٱلْبَاطِلِ وَتَكْتُمُونَ ٱلْحَقَّ﴾: if you said in ordinary speech: لِمَ تقومُ وتقعدَ يا رجل؟ ("Why do you stand up and [at the same time] sit down, man?") by ṣarf (divergence, i.e. the accusative of the verb after wāw), it would be permissible; so had (وتكتموا) been put in the accusative, it would have been correct.

farraa:72-72.t: His saying: ﴿وَقَالَتْ طَّآئِفَةٌ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَابِ آمِنُواْ بِٱلَّذِيۤ أُنْزِلَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ وَجْهَ ٱلنَّهَارِ﴾ means the dawn prayer, ﴿وَٱكْفُرُوۤاْ آخِرَهُ﴾ means the noon prayer. The Jews said this when the qibla was turned from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿba. The Jews said: "Pray the dawn prayer with Muḥammad — may Allah bless him and his Companions and grant them peace — and when it is noon, pray toward your own qibla, so as to make the Companions of Muḥammad doubt their qibla; for in their eyes you are more knowledgeable than they, and so they will return to your qibla."

farraa:73-73.t:
As for His saying: ﴿وَلاَ تُؤْمِنُوۤاْ إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ﴾, it is said that it is part of the saying of the Jews. He is saying: and do not believe [anyone] except one who follows your religion.
The lām is like [that in] His saying: ﴿عَسَى أَنْ يَكُونَ رَدِفَ لَكُمْ﴾, the meaning being: ردِفكم ("has come close behind you").
And His saying: ﴿أَن يُؤْتَىۤ أَحَدٌ مِّثْلَ مَآ أُوتِيتُمْ﴾: He is saying: do not believe that anyone is given the like of what you have been given. ﴿تؤمنوا﴾ is made to fall on ﴿أن يؤتى﴾, as if He said: "and do not believe that anyone is given the like of what you were given". That is one interpretation. It is also said: the speech of the Jews ended at His saying ﴿وَلاَ تُؤْمِنُوۤاْ إِلاَّ لِمَن تَبِعَ دِينَكُمْ﴾, and then the speech became His saying: "Say, O Muḥammad: guidance is the guidance of Allah, [lest] anyone be given the like of what the people of Islam have been given." (أن) came because His saying ﴿قُلْ إِنَّ ٱلْهُدَىٰ﴾ is like saying: "the clarification is the clarification of Allah" — He has made clear that no one is given the like of what the people of Islam have been given. And (أحد) is suitable [here] because the meaning of أن is the meaning of لا, as the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿يُبَيِّنُ اللهُ لَكُمْ أنْ تَضِلُّوا﴾, meaning: [so that] you do not go astray. And the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿كَذَلِكَ سَلَكْناهُ فِى قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمينَ. لاَيُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾: أن would be suitable in the place of لا.
And His saying ﴿أوْ يُحَاجُّوكُمْ عِنْد رَبِّكُمْ﴾ is in the sense of حتّى ("until") and in the sense of إلاّ ("unless"); as you say in ordinary speech: تعلَّقْ به أبدا أو يعطيَك حقّك ("cling to him forever, until/unless he gives you your due"); so حتّى and إلاّ are suitable in the place of أو.

farraa:75-75.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمِنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَابِ مَنْ إِن تَأْمَنْهُ بِقِنْطَارٍ يُؤَدِّهِ إِلَيْكَ﴾: al-Aʿmash and ʿĀṣim used to make the hāʾ quiescent (jazm) in يؤدِّه, and in "نُولِّهْ ما تَوَلّى", "أرجِهْ وأخاه", "خيرا يرهْ" and "شرا يرهْ". There are two explanations of this for them. One of them is that these people supposed that the jussive is on the hāʾ, whereas it is only on what precedes the hāʾ; and this, being a misconception, is an error. The other is that some of the Arabs make the hāʾ quiescent when what precedes it is vowelled, so they say ضربتهْ ضربا شديدا ("I struck him hard"); or one leaves the hāʾ quiescent, its original vowel being ḍamma, like رأيتهم and أنتم — do you not see that the mīm is quiescent while its origin is ḍamma? And some of the Arabs give the hāʾ a vowel without wāw, saying ضربتهُ (without wāw) ضربا شديدا. The more common way is to extend it with a wāw, so it is said كلمتهو كلاما ("I spoke to him"), on this pattern. The poet said, dropping the wāw:
أنا ابن كِلاب وابن أوْس فمن يكنْ * قِناعهُ مَغْطِيّا فإنّى لمُجْتَلَى
(I am the son of Kilāb and the son of Aws; whoever has his veil drawn over him — I, for my part, am plain to see.)
But when what precedes the hāʾ is quiescent, they prefer to drop the wāw from the hāʾ, saying: دَعْهُ يذهب ("let him go"), منْه and عنْه. They hardly ever say منهو or عنهو, extending it with a wāw when what precedes it is quiescent. That is because they cannot make the hāʾ quiescent when a quiescent letter precedes it; so when it became vowelled and could not be made quiescent, they were content with its vowel instead of the wāw.
And His saying ﴿إِلاَّ مَا دُمْتَ عَلَيْهِ قَآئِماً﴾: He is saying: as long as you keep pressing him for payment. The explanation of that is that when the people of Islam traded with the People of the Book, some of them would render what was entrusted, and some of them said: "The unlettered (al-ummiyyūn) — and they are the Arabs — have no inviolability like the inviolability of the people of our religion." So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed [us] that among them are trustworthiness and treachery, and the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ عَلَى اللَّهِ ٱلْكَذِبَ﴾, regarding their deeming it lawful to make off with the rights of the Muslims.

farraa:79-79.t:
His saying: ﴿بِمَا كُنتُمْ تُعَلِّمُونَ ٱلْكِتَابَ وَبِمَا كُنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ﴾ is read تُعلِّمون and تَعْلَمون. It came in the exegesis: by your reading the scriptures and your knowledge of them.
So the proper way would be (تَعْلَمون); but al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza read (تُعَلِّمون), because both "he teaches" and "he knows" apply to the learned man.

farraa:80-80.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يَأْمُرَكُمْ﴾: most of the readers read it in the accusative, referring it back to ﴿أَنْ يُؤْتِيَهُ اللهُ﴾: "nor that he should command you". In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (ولن يأمركم), and this is evidence that it is cut off from the coordination (nasaq) and is a fresh beginning. So, since (لا) stands in the place of (لن), it is put in the nominative, as the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿إِنّا أرْسَلْناكَ بالْحَقِّ بَشِيراً ونَذِيراً وَلا تُسْأَلُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ الْجَحِيم﴾, which in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh is (ولن تسأل), and in the reading of Ubayy (وما تُسأل عن أصحاب الجحيم).

farraa:81-81.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ أَخَذَ ٱللَّهُ مِيثَاقَ ٱلنَّبِيِّيْنَ لَمَآ آتَيْتُكُم مِّن كِتَابٍ وَحِكْمَةٍ﴾ — and لِما آتيتكم: Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read it with kasra on the lām, meaning: He took the covenant for those to whom He gave [the Book]; then he made His saying ﴿لَتُؤْمِنُنَّ بِهِ﴾ part of the taking [of the covenant], as you say: أخذتُ ميثاقك لتعمَلَنّ ("I took your covenant that you will surely act"), because taking a covenant is like making someone swear. Whoever gives the lām of (لما) fatḥa makes the lām a redundant (zāʾida) lām: since it has been placed on a conditional (jazāʾ) which has been given the form of a verb, and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) has been given the lām, إن, لا and ما, it is as if the lām were an oath, since it came to be met with the answer of an oath. And that is the proper way of the speech. «[Translator's note: the source prints يجواب and ويما, evidently misprints for بجواب and وبما; translated accordingly.]»

farraa:83-83.t: His saying: ﴿أَفَغَيْرَ دِينِ ٱللَّهِ يَبْغُونَ وَلَهُ أَسْلَمَ مَن فِي ٱلسَّمَاوَاتِ وَٱلأَرْضِ طَوْعاً وَكَرْهاً﴾: the people of the heavens submitted willingly. As for the people of the earth, since the established practice concerning them was that they be fought if they did not submit, they submitted willingly and unwillingly.

farraa:91-91.t:
His saying: ﴿فَلَن يُقْبَلَ مِنْ أَحَدِهِم مِّلْءُ ٱلأَرْضِ ذَهَباً﴾: you put الذهب in the accusative because it is an explicative (mufassir, i.e. tamyīz (specification)), the like of which only comes indefinite. So its accusative came out like the accusative in your saying: عندى عشرون درهما ("I have twenty dirhams") and لك خيرهما كبشا ("you have the better of the two as a ram"). Similar to it is His saying ﴿أوْ عَدْلُ ذلك صِيَاماً﴾. It is put in the accusative only because it issues from the measure you see mentioned before it, such as ملء الأرض or عَدْل ذلك: العَدْل is a known measure, and ملء الأرض is a known measure. So put in the accusative whatever comes to you on this pattern, [after] what is annexed to something having a measure; as when you say: عندى قدر قَفِيز دقيقا ("I have a qafīz-measure of flour"), قدر حَمْلةٍ تبْنا ("a load of straw"), قدر رطلين عسلا ("two raṭls of honey"). These are known measures, and what comes after them comes out as an explicative, because you see the explanation issuing from the description, indicating the kind of the measure — of what thing it is; just as when you say عندى عشرون ("I have twenty"), you have reported an unknown number whose statement is complete, but its kind is unknown and its explanation remains, so this became its explicative, and therefore it is put in the accusative.
Had you put it in the nominative as a fresh beginning, it would be permissible; as you say: عندى عشرون ("I have twenty"), and then you say afterwards: رجالٌ ("men"). Likewise if you said: مِلْء الأرض, then said: ذَهَبٌ, informing without connection.
And His saying: ﴿وَلَوِ ٱفْتَدَىٰ بِهِ﴾: the wāw here may be dispensed with; had it been said مِلْء الأرض ذهبا لو افتدى به, it would have been correct. It is like His saying: ﴿ولِيكون مِن الموقِنِين﴾; the wāw here is as though it had an implied verb after it.

farraa:93-93.t: His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ مَا حَرَّمَ إِسْرَائِيلُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ﴾: it is mentioned in the exegesis that he was afflicted with sciatica, and he bound himself, if he recovered, to forbid himself the food and drink he loved most. When he recovered, he forbade himself the flesh and milk of camels, which were the food and drink he loved most.

farraa:96-96.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّ أَوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ﴾: He is saying: the first mosque set up for people ﴿لَلَّذِي بِبَكَّةَ﴾. It was named بَكّة only because of the crowding of people in it; it is said بَكَّ الناسُ بعضُهم بعضا when they crowd one another.
And His saying: ﴿هُدىً﴾ is in the position of the accusative, following المبارك. It is said that it was called "blessed" (مباركا) only because it is a [means of] forgiveness of sins.

farraa:97-97.t:
His saying: ﴿فِيهِ آيَاتٌ بَيِّـنَاتٌ﴾: it is said that the signs are the Station (al-Maqām), the Ḥijr and the Ḥaṭīm. Ibn ʿAbbās read "فيه آية بيِّنة", making the Station alone the sign.
And His saying: ﴿وَمَن كَفَرَ﴾: He is saying: whoever says "Pilgrimage is not incumbent on me" — he denies its obligation by disbelief, not [merely] neglects it.

farraa:99-99.t: His saying: ﴿مَنْ آمَنَ تَبْغُونَهَا﴾: He means the path (السبيل), and made it feminine; the meaning is تبغون لها ("you seek for it [crookedness]"). Likewise ﴿يبغونكم الفِتنة﴾: they seek sedition for you. The Arabs say: ابغنى خادما فارِها ("seek me a sprightly servant"), meaning: seek it for me. When they mean "seek with me and help me in seeking it", they say أَبْغنى (giving fatḥa to the first alif, from بغيت, and to the second, from أبغيت). Likewise they say: المِسنى نارا and ألمِسنى, احلبنى and أَحلبنى, احْمِلنى and أحملنى, اعكمنى and أعكمنى. His saying احلِبنى means: milk for me, i.e. spare me the milking; and أحلبنى: help me with it. The rest of them follow this pattern.

farraa:103-103.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱعْتَصِمُواْ بِحَبْلِ ٱللَّهِ جَمِيعاً﴾: Arabic speech is like this, with the bāʾ; but sometimes the Arabs drop the bāʾ and say اعتصمت بك and اعتصمتك ("I held fast to you"). One of them said:
إذا أنت جازيت الإخاءَ بمثله * وآسيتنى ثم اعتصمتَ حباليا
(If you repay brotherhood with its like, and console me, and then hold fast to my ropes...)
So he dropped the bāʾ. It is like your saying: تعلَّقت زيدا and تعلقت بزيد ("I clung to Zayd"). One of them recited:
تعلَّقت هندا ناشئا ذات مِئزَرٍ * وأنت وقد قارَفْتَ لم تَدْر ما الحلُمْ
(You became attached to Hind as a youth, she wearing a waist-wrapper, and you — though nearing it — did not know what puberty was.)

farraa:106-106.t:
His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَبْيَضُّ وُجُوهٌ وَتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾: none of the readers put the verb in the masculine, as was said in ﴿لن ينال الله لحومها ولا دماؤها﴾ and His saying ﴿لا يحِلّ لك النِساء مِن بعد﴾. The masculine was made easy in these two only because there is a negation with them; the meaning in it is: not one of the women is lawful for you, and nothing of their flesh reaches Allah; so the masculine goes by the meaning. That is not the case with الوجوه. But had the verb of الوجوه been masculine, as you say قام القوم ("the people stood up"), that would have been permissible.
And His saying: ﴿فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ أَكْفَرْتُمْ﴾: it may be said: (أمّا) must have the fāʾ as its answer, so where is it? It is said: it was with an implied "saying"; when the saying dropped, the fāʾ dropped with it. The meaning — and Allah knows best — is: as for those whose faces are blackened, it will be said: "Did you disbelieve?"; so the fāʾ dropped together with (فيقال). The saying may be implied, and there is much of it in the Book of Allah. Of that is His saying ﴿ولو ترى إِذِ المجرِمون ناكِسوا رءوسِهِم عِند ربهم ربنا أبصرنا وسمِعنا﴾ and His saying ﴿وإِذ يرفع إِبراهِيم القواعِد من البيت وإِسماعيل ربنا تقبل منا﴾, and in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "ويقولان ربَّنا".

farraa:108-108.t: His saying: ﴿تِلْكَ آيَاتُ ٱللَّهِ﴾ means: these are the verses of Allah. Its matter has been explained at the beginning of al-Baqara.

farraa:110-110.t: His saying: ﴿كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ﴾: in interpretation, [it means]: in the Preserved Tablet. Its meaning is: you are the best community; like His saying ﴿واذكروا إِذ كنتم قلِيلا فكثركم﴾ and ﴿إِذ أنتم قليل مستضعفون فى الأرض﴾. Implying كان in such cases and expressing it are the same.

farraa:111-111.t: His saying: ﴿يُوَلُّوكُمُ ٱلأَدْبَارَ﴾ is jussive because it is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ). ﴿ثُمَّ لاَ يُنصَرُونَ﴾ is nominative as a fresh beginning; also, because the verse-endings are in nūn, that is among what strengthens the nominative; as He said ﴿ولا يؤذن لهم فيعتذِرون﴾, putting it in the nominative, while the Blessed and Exalted said ﴿لا يقضى عليهِم فيموتوا﴾.

farraa:112-112.t:
His saying: ﴿إِلاَّ بِحَبْلٍ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ﴾: He is saying: unless they hold fast to a rope from Allah; so He left that implied. The poet said:
رأتنى بحبليها فصَدَّت مخافةً * وفى الحبل روعاء الفؤادِ فروق
(She saw me [coming] with her two ropes and turned away in fear; and in the rope was a skittish, timid-hearted one.)
He meant: أقبلْتُ بحبليها ("I came with her two ropes"). And another said:
حنتنِى حانياتُ الدهِر حتى * كأنى خاتِل أَدنو لِصَيدِ
قريبُ الخَطْـوِ يحسب من رآنى * ولست مقيَّدا أنى بِقَيْدِ
(The bending blows of time have bent me, until I seem a stalker creeping up on game; short of step, so that whoever sees me thinks — though I am not fettered — that I am in a fetter.)
He means: مقيَّدا بقيد ("fettered with a fetter").

farraa:113-113.t:
His saying: ﴿لَيْسُواْ سَوَآءً مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَابِ أُمَّةٌ قَآئِمَةٌ﴾: He mentioned one community and did not mention another after it, while the speech is built on an intended "other", because سواء ("equal") requires two or more.
الأمة is nominative in two ways. One of them is that you refer it back to سواء, as if you said: "An upright community and another, disbelieving, are not equal; among them is such a community and such a community." The Arabs allow themselves to leave one of two things implied when there is an indication of it in the speech. The poet said:
عصيت إليها القلب إنى لأمرها * سميع فما أَدرى أَرُشْد طِلابُها
(I disobeyed my heart for her sake; I am attentive to her bidding, and I do not know whether pursuing her is right guidance.)
and he did not say "or error" nor "or not", because the speech and the meaning are understood. Another said:
أراك فلا أدرى أهمّ هممته * وذو الهمّ قِدماً خاشع متضائِل
(I see you, and do not know whether it is a care you have taken on — and the man of cares has ever been humbled and shrunken.)
And another said:
وما أدرى إذا يمَّمت وجها * أريد الخير أيُّهما يلِينى
أألخير الذى أنا أبتغيه * أم الشرُّ الذى لا يأتلينى
(I do not know, when I set out in some direction seeking good, which of the two will come to me: the good that I seek, or the evil that never fails to seek me?)
From it is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿أمَّن هو قانِت آناء الليلِ ساجِدا وقائِما﴾, and He did not mention the one who is his opposite, because His saying ﴿قل هل يستوِى الذِين يعلمون والذِين لا يعلمون﴾ is an indication of what was left implied of that. «[Translator's note: the source announces two ways for the nominative of الأمة but states only the first explicitly.]»
And His saying: ﴿يَتْلُونَ آيَاتِ ٱللَّهِ آنَآءَ ٱللَّيْلِ وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ﴾: prostration (السجود) in this place is a name for the prayer, not for prostration, because recitation does not take place in prostration or in bowing.

farraa:118-118.t: His saying, Exalted: ﴿قَدْ بَدَتِ ٱلْبَغْضَآءُ مِنْ أَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "وقد بدا البغضاء من أفواههم", masculine, because البغضاء is a maṣdar (verbal noun), and when a maṣdar is feminine it is permissible to make its verb masculine if [the verb] comes first; like ﴿وأَخذ الذِين ظلموا الصيحةُ﴾ and ﴿قد جاءكم بينة مِن ربكم﴾ and the like.

farraa:119-119.t:
His saying: ﴿هَآأَنْتُمْ أُوْلاۤءِ﴾: when the Arabs come to a pronoun (makniyy) that is qualified by هذا, هاذان or هؤلاء, they separate (ها) from (ذا) and put the pronoun between them. That is in the sense of taqrīb (presentative "here is…"), not otherwise. They say: أين أنت؟ ("Where are you?"), and the speaker says: هأنذا ("here I am"); they hardly ever say: هذا أنا. Likewise the dual and the plural; and from it is ﴿هَآأَنْتُمْ أُوْلاۤءِ تُحِبُّونَهُمْ﴾. Sometimes they repeat (ها) and join it to ذا, هذان and هؤلاء, saying: ها أنت هذا and ها أنتم هؤلاء. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said in al-Nisāʾ: ﴿ها أنتم هؤلاءِ جادلتم عنهم﴾.
When the speech is not presentative, or is with an overt noun, they keep (ها) joined to ذا, saying: هذا هو ("this is he") and هذان هما ("these two are they"), when it is a statement in which each of the two is sufficed by the other without a verb. The presentative, however, must have a verb, because it is incomplete. They wished thereby to distinguish between the presentative sense and the sense of the proper noun [phrase].

farraa:120-120.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِن تَصْبِرُواْ وَتَتَّقُواْ لاَ يَضُرُّكُمْ كَيْدُهُمْ شَيْئاً﴾: if you wish, it is taken as jussive even though it appears with ḍamma, being like your saying to a man: مُدُّ يا هذا ("stretch, you!"). Had you given it fatḥa or kasra, it would be correct, because some Arabs say مُدِّ يا هذا; and the fatḥa is the most fitting in Arabic. And if you wish, you take it as nominative and take (لا) in the sense of ليس, putting it in the nominative while implying the fāʾ; as the poet said:
فإن كان لا يُرضِيك حتى تردَّنى * إلى قَطَرِىّ لا إخالك راضِيا
(If nothing will please you until you send me back to Qaṭarī, I do not think you will ever be pleased.)
Some of the readers read "لا يَضِرْكُمْ", taking it from الضَيْر (harm). Al-Kisāʾī claimed that he heard some of the people of al-ʿĀliya say: لا ينفعنى ذلك وما يضورنى ("that does not benefit me, nor does it harm me"); so had it been read "لا يضُرْكم" according to this dialect, it would be correct.

farraa:121-121.t:
His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ غَدَوْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِكَ تُبَوِّىءُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ مَقَاعِدَ لِلْقِتَالِ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "تبوّى للمؤمنين مقاعد للقتال". The Arabs do that; they say: رَدِفك and رَدف لك ("he followed close behind you"). Al-Farrāʾ said: al-Kisāʾī said: I heard one of the Arabs say: نقدت لها مائة, meaning نقدتها مائة ("I paid her a hundred in cash"), of a woman he married. And al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
أستغفر الله ذنبا لست مُحصِيَه * ربَّ العبادِ إليه الوجهُ والعمل
(I ask forgiveness of Allah for sins I cannot count — the Lord of the servants, to Whom [one turns] the face and the deeds.)
The [normal] speech is with the lām, as Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿واستغفِرِى لِذنبِك﴾ and ﴿فاستغفروا لِذنوبِهِم﴾. And he recited to me:
أستغفر الله من جِدّى ومن لعبى * وِزرِى وكلُّ امرِئٍ لا بدّ مُتَّزِرُ
(I ask forgiveness of Allah for my earnestness and my play — for my burden; and every man must bear a burden.)
He means: لوزرى. وزرى, when the lām is dropped, is in the position of the accusative. And al-Kisāʾī recited to me:
إن أَجْزِ علقمةَ بن سعدٍ سعيه * لا تلقنِى أَجزِى بسعى واحدِ
لأحبنى حُبَّ الصبِىِّ وضمَّنِى * ضمَّ الهدِىّ إِلى الكرِيم الماجِدِ
(If I repay ʿAlqama ibn Saʿd for his effort, you will not find me repaying a single effort; he loved me as a child is loved, and took me to himself as a noble, glorious man takes in one under his protection.)
He said (لأحبنى) only because he made the answer of إن, since it is conditional, like the answer of لو.

farraa:122-122.t: His saying: ﴿وَٱللَّهُ وَلِيُّهُمَا﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "والله ولِيُّهم"; he returned from the two to the plural, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿هذانِ خصمانِ اختصموا فِى ربهِم﴾ and as He said: ﴿وإِن طائِفتانِ مِن المؤمِنِين اقتتلوا﴾.

farraa:128-128.t: His saying: ﴿لَيْسَ لَكَ مِنَ ٱلأَمْرِ شَيْءٌ أَوْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ أَوْ يُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾: there are two ways for its accusative. If you wish, you make it coordinated with His saying: ﴿لِيَقْطَعَ طَرَفاً مِنَ الذِينَ كَفَرُوا أوْ يَكْبِتَهُمْ﴾, i.e. ﴿أَوْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ أَوْ يُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾. And if you wish, you make its accusative in the sense of حتَّى ("until"), as you say: لا أزال ملازِمك أو تعطِيَنِى ("I will keep sticking to you until you give me"), or إلا أن تعطِينى حقىّ ("unless you give me my due").

farraa:135-135.t: His saying: ﴿وَمَن يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهُ﴾: it may be said: [what comes before إلا] is definite, while what comes after إلا is put in the nominative by following what precedes it only when that is indefinite and accompanied by a negation, as in your saying: ما عندى أحد إلا أبوك ("there is no one with me except your father"). [The answer is that] the meaning of His saying ﴿وَمَن يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ إِلاَّ ٱللَّهُ﴾ is: no one forgives sins except Allah; so it was construed according to the meaning. This occurs in the Qur'an in more than one place.

farraa:140-140.t:
His saying: ﴿إِن يَمْسَسْكُمْ قَرْحٌ﴾ — and قُرْح. Most of the readers read it with fatḥa on the qāf. The companions of ʿAbd Allāh read قُرْح. It is as if القُرْح were the pain of the wounds, and القَرْح the wounds themselves. In its nature it is like His saying: ﴿أَسْكِنُوهنَّ مِن حَيْثُ سَكَنْتُم مِن وُجْدِكُم﴾ and وَجْدكُم; ﴿والّذِينَ لاَ يَجِدُونَ إلاَّ جُهْدَهُمْ﴾ and جَهْدهم; and ﴿لاَ يُكَلّفُ اللهُ نَفْساً إِلا وُسْعَهَا﴾ [and وَسْعها].
And His saying: ﴿وَلِيَعْلَمَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾: He comes to know the believer from the other, and the steadfast from the other.
This is in the manner of أىّ and مَنْ, as He said: ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ أَىُّ الْحِزْبَيْنِ أَحْصَى﴾. When you put in place of أىّ or مَن the word الذى or an alif and lām, you put it in the accusative by what falls on it, as Allah the Blessed said: ﴿فَلَيَعْلَمَنّ اللهُ الَّذِينَ صَدَقُوا وَلَيَعْلَمَنّ الكّاذِبِين﴾. That is permissible because in "الذى" and in the alif and lām there is the sense of مَنْ and أىّ, since both carry the sense of being distinguished by the verb.
But when you put in their place a noun that contains no verb, it does not bear this meaning. So it is not permissible to say: قد سألت فعلمت عبدالله ("I asked and came to know ʿAbd Allāh"), unless you mean: I came to know what he is. If you put with عبدالله a noun containing an indication of أىّ, that is permissible, as when you say: إنما سألت لأعلم عبدالله مِن زيد ("I only asked in order to know ʿAbd Allāh from Zayd"), i.e. to tell this one from that one. And the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿لم تَعْلَمُوهُمْ أَن تَطَئُوهُمْ﴾ may mean: you did not know their whereabouts; and it may mean: you did not know what they were, unbelievers or Muslims. And Allah knows best its interpretation.

farraa:141-141.t: His saying: ﴿وَلِيُمَحِّصَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾ means: Allah purges the sins from those who believe; ﴿وَيَمْحَقَ ٱلْكَافِرِينَ﴾: He diminishes them and annihilates them.

farraa:142-142.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَمَّا يَعْلَمِ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ جَاهَدُواْ مِنكُمْ وَيَعْلَمَ ٱلصَّابِرِينَ﴾: al-Ḥasan read "ويعلمِ الصابِرين" with kasra, meaning the jussive. The readers, however, read it in the accusative. This is what the grammarians call al-ṣarf (divergence), as in your saying: "لم آته وأُكرِمَهُ إلا استخفّ بى" ("I never came to him and honoured him without his slighting me"). «[Translator's note: the source has وتهو, a misprint for وهو.]» Al-ṣarf is when two verbs come together joined by wāw, thumma, fāʾ or aw, with a negation or a question at the beginning, and you see that that negation or question cannot be repeated in the coordinated part; that is al-ṣarf. Following [the first verb in its case] is permissible in it, because it is coordination in form; and it is put in the accusative since it is impossible for what was introduced at the beginning to be introduced in both. Do you not see that you say: لست لأبى إن لم أقتلك أو إن لم تسبقنى فى الأرض ("May I not be my father's son if I do not kill you — unless you outrun me in the land")?
Likewise they say: لا يسعُنى شىء ويضيقَ عنك ("nothing is wide enough for me while being too narrow for you"), and (لا) is not repeated with يضيق. This is the explanation of al-ṣarf.

farraa:143-143.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ كُنْتُمْ تَمَنَّوْنَ ٱلْمَوْتَ مِن قَبْلِ أَن تَلْقَوْهُ فَقَدْ رَأَيْتُمُوهُ وَأَنْتُمْ تَنظُرُونَ﴾: its meaning is: you saw the causes of death. This was on the day of Uḥud; it means the sword and similar weapons.

farraa:144-144.t:
His saying: ﴿أَفإِنْ مَّاتَ أَوْ قُتِلَ ٱنْقَلَبْتُمْ عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ﴾: every question that enters upon a conditional means that its answer contains a statement standing by itself, and the conditional is a condition for that statement; this is of that kind. You put it in the jussive, though its meaning is nominative, only because it comes after the conditional; as the poet said:
حلفت له إنْ تُدْلجِ اللَّيْلَ لاَ يَزَلْ * أَمَامكَ بَيْتٌ من بيُوتِىَ سائِرُ
(I swore to him: if you travel by night, a house of my houses [i.e. a poem of my verses] will keep going on ahead of you.)
So (لا يزل) is in the position of the nominative, except that it is put in the jussive because it comes after the conditional and has become like the answer. Had it been "أفإن مات أو قتل تنقلبون", both the jussive and the nominative would be permissible in it. Similar to it is ﴿أفإن مِتَّ فَهُمُ الخالدون﴾, the meaning being: are they the immortals if you die? And His saying: ﴿فكَيْفَ تَتَّقُون إِنْ كَفَرْتم يوما يَجْعَلُ الوِلدانَ شِيبا﴾: if you delayed it and said in ordinary speech: (فكيف إن كفرتم تتقون), both the nominative and the jussive would be permissible in تتقون.

farraa:146-146.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَأَيِّن مِّن نَّبِيٍّ قَاتَلَ مَعَهُ رِبِّيُّونَ كَثِيرٌ﴾: الربّيون are the thousands.
It is read قُتِل and قاتل. Whoever reads قُتل makes His saying ﴿فَمَا وَهَنُواْ لِمَآ أَصَابَهُمْ﴾ refer to those who remained; whoever reads قاتل makes the weakening refer to those who fought. This was mentioned only because on the day of Uḥud they said: "Muḥammad ﷺ has been killed," and they lost heart, and some of them turned hypocrite. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: ﴿وما محمد إِلاّ رسولٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ الرُّسُلُ﴾, and revealed: ﴿وَكَأَيِّن مِّن نَّبِيٍّ قَاتَلَ مَعَهُ رِبِّيُّونَ كَثِيرٌ﴾.
The meaning of وكأين is وكم ("how many").
Some of the exegetes said: "وكأين من نبى قُتِل" means: and "with him were many myriads", the verb falling on the prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He is saying: they did not turn back from their religion, nor did they desist after his being killed. And that is a good interpretation.

farraa:147-147.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَا كَانَ قَوْلَهُمْ إِلاَّ أَن قَالُواْ﴾: you put القول in the accusative by كان, and make أنْ in the position of the nominative. There is much like it in the Qur'an.
The best way is to make (أن) in the position of the nominative; but had القول and its like been put in the nominative, and the accusative been given to "أن", it would be correct. «[Translator's note: the source has صوبا, a misprint for صوابا "correct".]»

farraa:150-150.t: His saying: ﴿بَلِ ٱللَّهُ مَوْلاَكُمْ﴾ is nominative as a khabar (predicate); had you put it in the accusative — (بل أطيعوا الله مولاكم) ("rather, obey Allah, your Protector") — it would have been a good way.

farraa:152-152.t:
His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا فَشِلْتُمْ﴾: it is said that it involves something put first and something put later; its meaning is: "until, when you disputed about the matter, you lost heart". So this wāw is meant to be dropped, as it is said: ﴿فلمَّا أسلما وتَلَّه للْجَبِين. وناديْناه﴾, meaning: ناديناه ("We called him"). This is said with "حتى إذا" and "فلمَّا أن"; it has not come with anything other than these two. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿حتى إذا فُتِحتْ يأجوجُ ومأجوجُ وهُمْ مِن كل حَدَبٍ يَنْسِلون﴾, then He said: ﴿واقتربَ الوعدُ الحقُّ﴾, meaning: اقترب ("drew near"). And the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿حتى إِذا جاءوها وفُتِحت أبوابها﴾, and in another place: ﴿فتِحت﴾. And the poet said:
حتى إذا قَمِلت بطونُكُم * ورأيتُم أبناءكُمْ شَبُّوا
وقلبتُم ظهرَ المِجَنِّ لنا * إن اللئِيم العاجِزُ الخَبّ
(Until, when your bellies grew fat, and you saw that your sons had grown up, you turned the back of the shield against us — truly the base man is the feeble, the treacherous.)
الخَبّ is the treacherous one, and الخِبّ is treachery. As for His saying: ﴿إذا السماءُ انْشَقَّتْ. وَأَذِنَتْ لرَبِّها وحُقّت﴾ and His saying: ﴿وإِذا الأَرْضُ مُدَّتْ. وألْقَتْ ما فِيها وتَخَلّتْ﴾, it is a single utterance whose answer is in what comes after it, as if He were saying: "on that day he will meet his reckoning". One of the Basrans who narrated from Qatāda said: "إذا السَّماءُ انْشَقَّتْ. أذنت لربها وحُقَّت" [taking the answer as أذنت with the wāw dropped], but I do not favour that, because it is in the manner of ﴿إذا الشَّمسُ كُوِّرَتْ﴾ and ﴿إذا السَّماءُ انْفَطَرتْ﴾, whose answers come after them: ﴿عَلمَتْ نَفْسٌ ما أَحْضَرَتْ﴾ and ﴿وعلِمت نفس ما قدَّمت وأخَّرت﴾.

farraa:153-153.t:
His saying: ﴿إِذْ تُصْعِدُونَ وَلاَ تَلْوُونَ عَلَىٰ أحَدٍ﴾: الإصعاد is used for setting out on journeys and departures. You say: أصعدنا من مكة ("we set out from Mecca"), and from Baghdad to Khurāsān, and the like. But when you climb a ladder or a stair and the like, you say صعِدت and not أصعدت. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read: "إِذ تَصْعَدون ولا تلوون", treating climbing on the mountain like climbing a ladder.
And His saying: ﴿وَٱلرَّسُولُ يَدْعُوكُمْ فِيۤ أُخْرَاكُمْ﴾: some of the Arabs say أُخراتِكم, but it is not permissible in the Qur'an, because of the tāʾ it adds to the script of the Copies. The poet said:
ويتّقى السيف بأُخْراتِه * من دون كفّ الجارِ والمِعصمِ
(He wards off the sword with his rear, in defence of the protégé's hand and wrist.)
And His saying: ﴿فَأَثَابَكُمْ غَمّاًً بِغَمٍّ﴾: الإثابة ("rewarding") here is [in] the sense of punishment, but it is as the poet said:
أخاف زيادا أن يكون عطاؤه * أداهِمَ سُوداً أو مُحَدْرَجَةً سُمْرَا
(I fear that Ziyād's gift will be black fetters or tightly twisted brown [whips].)
A man who has wronged you may be told: لئن أتيتنى لأثِيبنّك ثوابك ("If you come to me, I will surely give you your reward"), meaning: I will surely punish you; and perhaps someone unacquainted with the ways of Arabic would deny it. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has said: ﴿فَبَشِّرْهُمْ بعذَابٍ أليم﴾, and good tidings are only for good, yet that has been said of evil.
The meaning of His saying ﴿غَمّاًً بِغَمٍّ﴾ is what befell them on the day of Uḥud of defeat and slaughter; then Khālid ibn al-Walīd appeared above them with his cavalry, and they feared him, and that grieved them.
And His saying: ﴿وَلاَ مَآ أَصَابَكُمْ﴾: (ما) is in the position of the genitive [coordinated] with "ما فاتكم", i.e. nor over what befell you.

farraa:154-154.t:
His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ أَنزَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِّن بَعْدِ ٱلْغَمِّ أَمَنَةً نُّعَاساً يَغْشَىٰ طَآئِفَةً مِّنْكُمْ﴾ is read with tāʾ, so that it refers to الأمنة (security), and with yāʾ, so that it refers to النعاس (slumber); like His saying ﴿يَغْلِى فى البُطون﴾ and تغلى: when it is (تغلى) it is the tree, and when it is (يغلِى) it refers to المُهْل (molten metal).
And His saying: ﴿يَغْشَىٰ طَآئِفَةً مِّنْكُمْ وَطَآئِفَةٌ قَدْ أَهَمَّتْهُمْ أَنْفُسُهُمْ﴾: you put الطائفة in the nominative by His saying (أهمتهم), through the pronoun that refers back to it; and if you wish, you put it in the nominative by His saying ﴿يَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ غَيْرَ ٱلْحَقِّ﴾. Had it been accusative, it would have been correct; like His saying in al-Aʿrāf: ﴿فَرِيقاً هَدَى وفَرِيقاً حَقّ عَلَيْهِم الضَّلاَلَةُ﴾.
When you see a noun with speech before it and a verb after it which has fallen on a pronoun referring back to it, both the nominative and the accusative are permissible in the noun. Of that is His saying: ﴿والسماءَ بَنَيْناها بِأَيْدٍ﴾ and His saying: ﴿والأرضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا فَنِعْمَ الْمَاهِدُون﴾; it may be accusative or nominative. Whoever puts it in the accusative treats the wāw as if it were a frame for the verb, connected to the verb; whoever puts it in the nominative assigns the wāw to the noun, and puts it in the nominative through the pronoun returning to it; as the poet said:
إن لَمَ اشفِ النفوسَ من حىِّ بَكْرٍ * وعدِىٌّ تطَاهُ جُرْبُ الجمِال
(If I do not heal [our] souls [by vengeance] on the tribe of Bakr — while ʿAdī is trampled by mangy camels...)
The Arabs hardly ever put something like (عدىّ) in this sense in the accusative, because the wāw cannot properly be transferred to the verb; do you not see that you do not say: وتطأ عدِيّا جُرْبُ الجِمال? So when you see that the wāw sits well with the noun, make the nominative the proper way of the speech; when you see that the wāw sits well with the verb, make the accusative the proper way; and when you see that what precedes the verb sits well with both verb and noun, make the nominative and accusative equal, neither prevailing over the other; as in the poet's saying:
إذا ابنَ أبِى موسى بِلالاً أتيته * فقام بفأسٍ بين وُِصْلَيْكَ جازِر
(When you come to Ibn Abī Mūsā, Bilāl, then may a butcher stand with an axe between your two joints.)
The nominative and accusative in this are equal.
As for the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وأمّا ثمودُ فَهَدَيْناهم﴾, the proper way in it is the nominative, because أمّا sits well with the noun and does not occur with the verb.
